Conversational analytics, powered by
Gemini for Google Cloud
, lets you investigate your data by asking questions about it in conversational language through an intuitive chat interface. Conversational analytics provides multiple ways to "converse" with your data. When using Conversational Analytics with Explore data, you can ask questions about a single Explore in a conversation or create an Explore data agent to chat with as many as five Explores at once. You can also use Explore data agents that other users have created and shared with you.
Note:
This page refers to Explore data agents — data agents that query Explores. For information about data agents that query user-defined and LookML dashboards, see the
Query a user-defined dashboard with a dashboard agent
and
Create and manage data agents for LookML dashboards
documentation pages, respectively.
This page discusses how to use Conversational Analytics to engage with Explore data. It covers the following topics:
Starting a conversation with a single Explore
Start a conversation with an existing data agent that queries Explores
Asking questions about your data
Managing queries within a conversation
Understanding query results and calculations
Managing conversations
Learn
how and when Gemini
for Google Cloud uses your data
.
As an early-stage technology, Gemini for Google Cloud
products can generate output that seems plausible but is factually incorrect. We recommend that you
validate all output from Gemini for Google Cloud products before you use it.
For more information, see
Gemini for Google Cloud and responsible AI
.
Before you begin
Before you can use Conversational Analytics to engage with your Explore data, make sure that the
setup and requirements for your Looker instance
have been satisfied and that you have been granted the
appropriate permissions
to perform the tasks that are described on this page.
Start a conversation with a single Explore
To start a conversation — a discrete set of questions and answers about your data in regular, natural language in a chat interface — with a single Explore, follow these steps:
Navigate to the Conversational Analytics interface.
From the
main navigation menu
: Select
Conversations
. Select the
Explores
tab and then select the Explore that you want to query.
From the
Create
menu
: Select
Conversation
. Select the
Explores
tab and then select the Explore that you want to query.
From a
Looker Explore
: Select
Start a conversation
. This option isn't available if you're using the
new Explore experience
.
By default the conversation is called "Untitled." After you ask your first question in the conversation, Conversational Analytics automatically generates a conversation title that's based on your question and response. To change the generated name, click the title at the top of the conversation page and enter a new conversation name. To save your changes, click elsewhere on the page, or press return (Mac) or Enter (PC).
Once you have created a conversation, you can
ask questions
about the data in the
send_spark
Ask a question
field within the conversation. You can return to the conversation from the
schedule
Recent Conversations
section.
Start a conversation with an existing data agent that queries Explores
Note:
To create a new data agent to chat with Explore data, see the
Create and manage Explore data agents
documentation page. To query a user-defined or LookML dashboard with a data agent, see the
Query a user-defined dashboard with a dashboard agent
and
Create and manage data agents for LookML dashboards
documentation pages, respectively.
Data agents are customized with context and instructions that are specific to your data. You can start a conversation with an existing
data agent that you created
or that another user has
shared with you
. To start a conversation with an existing data agent that's connected to up to five Looker Explores follow these steps:
Navigate to the Conversational Analytics interface.
From the
main navigation menu
: Select
Conversations
. Select the
Agents
tab and then select the Explore data agent that you want to converse with.
From the
Create
menu
: Select
Conversation
. Select the
Agents
tab and then select the Explore data agent that you want to converse with.
By default the conversation is called "Untitled." After you ask your first question in the conversation, Conversational Analytics automatically generates a conversation title that's based on your question and response. To change the generated name, click the title at the top of the conversation page and enter a new conversation name. To save your changes, click elsewhere on the page, or press return (Mac) or Enter (PC).
Once you have created a conversation, you can
ask questions
about the data in the
send_spark
Ask a question
field within the conversation. You can return to the conversation from the
schedule
Recent Conversations
section.
Ask questions about Looker data
When you're beginning a new conversation, Conversational Analytics suggests some starting questions to ask. The questions don't need to be in a specific format or use a specific syntax. However, they do need to relate to the Explore that you've selected.
Type your question in natural language into the
Ask a question
field. Select a
question mode
and click
send
.
After you submit your query, you can cancel Conversational Analytics's response by clicking
stop
Stop response
. Conversational analytics stops running the query and displays the following message:
The query was cancelled.
For more guidance on the types of questions that you can ask, see
Limitations on questions
.
Select a question mode
When you ask a question, you can select the question mode from a drop-down menu that contains the following options:
Fast
(default): Best for most questions.
Thinking
: Detailed reasoning.
Conversational analytics defaults to
Fast
question mode. Conversational analytics will maintain the same question mode throughout any
multi-turn conversations
, unless you manually change it.
Fast mode
Fast
mode is recommended for most questions and is selected by default. In
Fast
mode, Conversational Analytics maps your natural language query directly to the LookML parameters that are defined in the LookML models that underlie your conversation's Explores. Conversational analytics responds quickly without spending extra tokens on thinking or streaming thoughts summaries in the chat.
Queries in
Fast
mode provide the same level of accuracy as queries in
Thinking
mode. Use
Fast
mode for your questions unless you specifically want to see the agent's reasoning process.
Thinking mode
In
Thinking
mode, the agent spends additional tokens thinking through the request and streams a thoughts summary directly in the chat while processing your query, giving you visibility into the agent's
detailed reasoning
steps.
Although
Thinking
mode does not produce more accurate answers than
Fast
mode, displaying the agent's reasoning lets you observe how Conversational Analytics interprets your query, plans its analytical steps, and references the underlying LookML models.
Select
Thinking
mode if you want to inspect the agent's detailed reasoning steps or test how an agent interacts with your data sources, and you want to spend the additional tokens required for thinking.
How Conversational Analytics processes your questions
Conversational Analytics may rephrase your question after you've submitted a query, and the rephrased question will be displayed in the conversation window following your original question. For example, Conversational Analytics might rephrase the question "What is the mean of user ages?" to "What is the average user age?"
While Conversational Analytics runs your query, you can
observe its reasoning
and thought process. Conversational analytics may ask follow-up questions to clarify any ambiguities in the original query. For example, if there are multiple, similarly named fields, Conversational Analytics may ask you to clarify which field is most appropriate to use in processing your query.
Multi-turn conversations
Conversational Analytics will take previous questions and answers into account as you continue the conversation. You can take previous answers and build on them by further refining results or changing the visualization type.
Important:
You can only reference previous questions in answers from the active conversation. You cannot reference previous questions and answers from other conversations.
For more guidance on creating questions, see
Limitations on questions
.
Clarifying questions
While Conversational Analytics runs your query, you can
observe its reasoning
and thought process. Conversational analytics may ask follow-up questions to clarify any ambiguities in the original query. For example, if there are multiple, similarly named fields, Conversational Analytics may ask you to clarify which field is most appropriate to use in processing your query.
Conversation metadata
When you converse with an Explore or a data agent, the collapsible
storage
Data
panel shows the name of the Looker Explore that's being used by the conversation. The
storage
Data
panel also provides the following options:
open_in_new
View fields
: When chatting with an Explore, you can view the Explore in a new browser window by clicking
open_in_new
View fields
.

items.title: Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes The google/adk-recipes repository unifies Agent Development Kit (ADK) resources into three structured layers—core/, plugins/, a
items.content:
Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes
- Google Developers Blog
Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes
OCT. 15, 2026
Pier Paolo Ippolito
Product Manager
Shahin Saadati
Software Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
The curated library of ADK recipes powering Google Cloud's Agents CLI, Agent Garden, and Gemini Enterprise app.
Introduction
A developer building on Google Cloud today can scaffold a long-horizon memory agent from the terminal, install a retail vertical skill into a coding assistant with one line, and deploy a fully-wired production service to Cloud Run, Agent Runtime, Agent Garden, or Gemini Enterprise app — all from the same curated source tree. That tree is
google/adk-recipes
, the restructured successor to
google/adk-samples
that now serves Agent Platform from a single source of truth.
ADK recipes are agent-friendly: we've made it easy for your agents to 1) discover relevant recipes for various agent use cases, and 2) install and use them automatically from your favorite harness.
google/adk-recipes
splits its content into three top-level folders:
core/
for reference patterns curated by the Agents CLI and DevRel teams, plugins/ for installable vertical skills packaged as Plugin Recipes conforming to the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 spec, and contrib/ for end-to-end deployable services across five languages. Every piece has been designed with machine readability as the primary consideration.
What follows is a walkthrough of the
repository
's shape, three worked examples (one per layer), and a reflection on what the new structure enables.
What's in the repo
Three top-level roots, each anchored on one reader action:
Every recipe ships a validated
manifest.yaml
, an
AGENTS.md
that tells the coding assistant opening it what the recipe is and how to use it, and (for
contrib/
and
plugins/
) a
Dockerfile
plus a runnability test. CI enforces the standards on every PR, and a suite of coding-assistant skills in the repo (
prepare-python-recipe
,
generate-manifest
,
github-pr-review
, and others) does most of the preparation, so your agent can scaffold, validate, and submit a recipe end-to-end.
Built for coding assistants, not just developers
Every
AGENTS.md
, every
manifest.yaml
, every
SKILL.md
is written primarily for the AI coding assistant that will open the repo on your behalf;
README.md
files are what humans still read. The handbook glossary captures the dual framing:
"Recipe — a runnable agent example (or importable agent module) under
core/
,
contrib/
, or
plugins/
, consumed by ADK developers and coding agents alike."
What it powers across the Agent Platform
adk-recipes
serves as the single source of truth for ADK content across the three Agent Platform surfaces that consume it. Each reads the repository through its own protocol.
Agents CLI reads
core/
. When a developer runs
uvx --from google-agents-cli agents-cli create my-agent
, Agents CLI can scaffold on demand a
core/
recipe. The CLI, launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next, exposes the full scaffold → deploy → evaluate → publish lifecycle; the base content it serves comes from our recipes. Horizon, the reference harness we examine below, is an example pattern Agents CLI treats as a production template.
Agent Garden features a curated selection. The developer-facing path into the repository is a pull request to
contrib/
: a recipe lands in GitHub, becomes part of the public ADK ecosystem, and from that moment is discoverable by other developers and by coding assistants reading the repository. Appearing in the Agent Garden gallery is a separate editorial decision made by the Agent Garden team, which curates a subset of recipes and promotes them to the public catalog on their own cadence. Once an agent is in the gallery, any developer in a Google Cloud project gets a one-click install.
Beyond these primary surfaces, Google Cloud's own infrastructure components appear as building blocks inside the recipes themselves. Horizon uses Agent Platform Sandboxes for per-user sandboxing, Memory Bank for durable memory, and Agent Platform Sessions for session state. The retail product-search Plugin Recipe uses Vector Search 2.0 on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform paired with BigQuery. The retail virtual-tryon Plugin Recipe uses Gemini image models for still composites and Veo 3.1 Reference-to-Video for animated outputs. The recipes do not just live alongside Agent Platform; they document it in use.
For developers working with coding assistants outside Google Cloud's tooling (Claude Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Windsurf, Zed, and others), Plugin Recipes additionally install through the open
npx skills
CLI maintained by vercel-labs.
Horizon: a reference pattern for
core/
Building an agent that can handle a single conversation is a well-understood problem. Building one that holds its own across days of interaction, remembering what the user did yesterday and planning tasks for tomorrow, is a materially different undertaking. The hard parts of such a long-horizon system are the same regardless of what the agent is being built to do: cross-session memory, per-user sandboxing of tool execution, secrets management, guardrails against runaway behaviour, and the orchestration primitives that make multi-step tasks resumable. Horizon, which lives at
core/python/long-horizon-harness
, is the reference harness we built to collect these primitives in one place.
The shortest path from a fresh clone to a running Horizon instance:
uvx google-agents-cli setup
gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID
gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/google/adk-recipes.git
cd adk-recipes
git sparse-checkout set core/python/long-horizon-harness
cd core/python/long-horizon-harness
# Default: LHA_ENVIRONMENT_BACKEND=local, in-memory sessions, no cloud deploys needed
make dev-local
Plain text
Copied
make deploy
rolls the backend to Cloud Run through Terraform; make destroy tears it back down. Horizon's evaluation suite lives in
tests/eval/evalsets/
as eighteen named behavioural rubrics covering memory recall, injection-based exfiltration attempts, guardrail halting under adversarial input, tool-selection discipline, and a journey-level plot-artifact evaluation. The rubrics are executed with
uv run pytest tests/eval
.
A first chat turn against the running backend confirms the memory layer is wired correctly:
Horizon is the harness we give coding assistants to study before building something harder. When a developer asks their assistant to build an agent that must run across days of interaction, the right next step is
uvx google-agents-cli create
with Horizon as the scaffold, and the rest of the harness falls into place.
The retail Plugin Recipe
Horizon encodes a reference pattern. It does not encode a vertical. For that, the second layer of the repository holds Plugin Recipes, each addressing a specific industry domain. The first vertical fully covered in this launch is retail, available under
plugins/retail/
.
The Plugin Recipe format sits on top of the Agent Plugins v1.0.0 specification published at
agent-plugins.org
, an open standard for packaging installable AI skills across coding assistants. The specification defines a plugin as a bundle of one or more skills with a top-level
plugin.json
manifest declaring name, version, license, and ownership. Each skill is a self-contained folder with a
SKILL.md
conversational installer, a
README.md
, an
EVAL.yaml
of quality gates, and the scripts and assets the skill needs to do its work. The retail plugin's layout is:
plugins/retail/
├── plugin.json
└── skills/
├── product-search/
│   ├── SKILL.md       # Q-MODE conversational installer
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── EVAL.yaml      # LLM-as-judge rubrics + deterministic assertions
│   ├── scripts/
│   ├── references/
│   └── assets/
└── virtual-tryon/
└── ...
Plain text
Copied
Two skills ship in this plugin today. The first,
retail-product-search
, builds an ADK agent with a vector-search retrieval tool backed by Vector Search 2.0 on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and a BigQuery catalog. The skill handles the entire pipeline: ingesting a CSV or JSON catalog into BigQuery, generating multimodal and text embeddings with Vertex AI Embeddings, building the Vector Search collection, scaffolding the ADK agent with a
retrieve_docs
tool, and deploying to Cloud Run. The agent is deliberately single-agent: one
root_agent
with one retrieval tool and no coordinator layer. The semantic complexity sits in the retrieval pipeline and the evaluator rubric, not in agent-to-agent communication; adding orchestration layers would obscure the pattern rather than clarify it.
The second skill,
retail-virtual-tryon
, generates a photorealistic composite of a model wearing or holding a product, with an optional eight-second studio catwalk video on top. It uses
gemini-2.5-flash-image
by default, falling back to
gemini-2.5-pro-image
when editorial quality matters more than latency. For video it uses
veo-3.1-generate-001
in Reference-to-Video mode, conditioning the generated motion on the still produced by the image pipeline. The skill ships a pre-flight product-cutout classifier and configurable safety levels, operational details that become obvious after the third real production deployment.
Both skills install into any coding assistant that reads skills with a single command:
# From Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor …
npx skills add google/adk-recipes --skill retail-product-search --full-depth
npx skills add google/adk-recipes --skill retail-virtual-tryon --full-depth
Plain text
Copied
The
--full-depth
flag instructs the CLI to walk past its default top-level lookup and discover the nested
plugins/retail/skills/
structure. The install lands in
~/.agents/skills/<skill-name>/
and is symlinked into every detected coding assistant on the local machine:
$ npx skills add google/adk-recipes --skill retail-product-search --full-depth -g
●  claude-code_2-1-288_agent  Agent detected — installing non-interactively
◇  Source: https://github.com/google/adk-recipes.git
◇  Repository cloned
◇  Found 11 skills
●  Installing to: Antigravity CLI, Augment, IBM Bob, Claude Code, OpenClaw,
CodeBuddy, Continue, Crush, Droid, Goose, Junie, iFlow CLI,
Kilo Code, Kiro CLI, Kode, MCPJam, Mux, OpenHands, Qoder, Qwen Code,
Roo Code, Trae, Windsurf, Zencoder, …
◇  Installation Summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  ~/.agents/skills/retail-product-search                                │
│    universal: Antigravity CLI, Droid, Kilo Code, Amp +15   │
│    symlink → Augment, IBM Bob, Claude Code, OpenClaw, CodeBuddy +25    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
◇  Installed 1 skill
└  Done!  Review skills before use; they run with full agent permissions.
Plain text
Copied
The skill ecosystem is designed to compose. The
retail-product-search SKILL.md
instructs the host coding assistant to pull two companion skills from
google/skills
if they are not already installed, keeping cross-cutting concerns like BigQuery basics and Gemini API usage in one place and reusable by multiple vertical plugins.
Once installed, the coding assistant reads
SKILL.md
and initiates a Q-MODE interview. For
retail-product-search
, Quick Start is two questions (GCP project ID and the path to product data, with sensible defaults for both); Full Setup adds two more covering product-fields level and GCP region. By the end of the interview the skill has written a
./design-spec.md
reflecting the project's actual shape and executed
scripts/setup.py
to land the catalog in BigQuery, generate the embeddings, build the Vector Search collection, and run
EVAL.yaml
against the result. If the rubric and assertion checks fall below the 80 percent passing target, the skill halts and surfaces the specific failures.
An end-to-end setup run on the bundled five-product demo catalog produces:
$ .venv/bin/python scripts/setup.py --config ./design-spec.md
INFO:__main__: SETUP PIPELINE (driven by design-spec.md)
INFO:__main__:   Project:      testproject-425813

INFO:__main__:   Validating sample data... Validated 5 records.
INFO:__main__:   Ingesting into BigQuery...
INFO:ingest_bigquery: Creating dataset testproject-425813.retail_skill_products
INFO:ingest_bigquery: Loaded 5 valid products
INFO:__main__:   Creating Vector Search collection...
INFO:ingest_vertex_search: Collection created successfully
INFO:ingest_vertex_search: Ingestion complete: 5 created, 0 skipped, 0 errors

Copied
A live retrieval against the collection the skill has just provisioned returns:

>>> retrieve_docs("wireless headphones under 200")

items.title: Announcing DPoP Support for Google OAuth: Securing Refresh Tokens Google OAuth Platform now supports DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) to sender-constrain refresh tokens, ne
items.content:
Announcing DPoP Support for Google OAuth: Securing Refresh Tokens
- Google Developers Blog
Announcing DPoP Support for Google OAuth: Securing Refresh Tokens
OCT. 15, 2026
Sergei Akulich
Product Manager
Brian Daugherty
Product Solutions Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Traditional OAuth bearer tokens operate on a "finders-keepers" model, making them vulnerable to Infostealer malware (e.g. RedLine, NodeStealer) and Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks.
DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) is an application-layer OAuth 2.0 security profile (
RFC 9449
) that neutralizes token theft and replay attacks by cryptographically binding tokens to a client-generated asymmetric keypair at the application layer, ensuring that even if a token is stolen, it cannot be replayed without the corresponding private key.
This article is meant to inform you on where and how to
adopt DPoP
and describes Google's specific DPoP implementation. A DPoP adoption
SKILL.md
is also available to help implement DPoP.
Some optional features and implementation decisions in RFC 9449 are delegated to Google as an authorization provider.
Google Identity
, and its
OAuth Platform
, function as a developer-facing service where engineers implement OAuth 2.0 and cryptographic security controls like DPoP to protect API integrations. Separately, Google Workspace
Context-Aware Access
(CAA) leverages DPoP to secure enterprise AI workloads on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform by cryptographically validating agent identities at the Agent Gateway.
Google's OAuth Platform supports DPoP binding specifically for refresh tokens. This design choice reflects a pragmatic engineering tradeoff: by sender-constraining the long-lived refresh token, we neutralize the primary vector for persistent offline impersonation. Meanwhile, short-lived access tokens remain standard Bearer tokens, ensuring that high-QPS resource APIs do not incur the per-request asymmetric cryptographic verification overhead of DPoP. This approach delivers robust protection for your most sensitive credentials while maintaining the high performance and low latency of Google API integrations.
Unlike standard Bearer token flows, DPoP requires client-side cryptographic key generation, strict timestamp and nonce handling, specific claim computation (htm, htu, iat, jti), exact header construction, and DPoP proof JWT construction. These changes may introduce additional system constraints to support secure computation, handling, and storage.
Architectural considerations
The IETF’s Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security (
RFC 9700
) discusses sender-constrained refresh tokens. Additionally, the
OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications
IETF draft discusses three models: Backend-for-Frontend (BFF), Token-Mediating Backend, and Browser-based OAuth Client.
Following this guidance, Google recommends using DPoP to sender-contrain refresh tokens in these models.
Unlike transport-layer token binding (e.g., mTLS/RFC 8705) which often breaks or terminates at modern cloud proxies and load balancers, DPoP operates at the HTTP header level. This makes it highly resilient for complex, multi-hop environments, including emerging
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
and autonomous agent architectures.
Architectural Deep-Dive: The Performance-vs-Security Tradeoff
A common question from security architects is: If DPoP is designed to sender-constrain tokens, why are Google's access tokens still standard Bearer tokens?
The answer lies in operational scaling and performance at Google's scale. Verifying asymmetric cryptographic signatures (such as ES256) requires significant CPU cycles. If every API call to high-throughput Google resource servers (like Gmail, Calendar, or Drive APIs) required verifying a DPoP proof, the compute overhead at the API Gateway layer would be massive, introducing measurable latency and scaling costs.
By constraining DPoP binding strictly to the refresh token, Google's architecture achieves a balance:
Long-Lived Credentials Protected:
The highly sensitive, long-lived refresh token (which can be used to obtain new access tokens indefinitely) is cryptographically bound to the client's key pair. If exfiltrated, it is useless to an attacker.
High-Performance Serving:
Short-lived access tokens (typically valid for 1 hour or less) remain standard Bearer tokens. This ensures that the vast majority of API requests incur zero cryptographic verification overhead, maintaining the high performance and low latency developers expect from Google APIs.
Complementary Protections: DPoP and DBSC
DPoP is a powerful tool for securing OAuth 2.0 tokens, but it is important to understand its boundaries.
DPoP does not protect standard web application session cookies, which remain a primary target for Infostealer malware. To address cookie theft, Google and the Web Incubator Community Group (WICG) are actively developing
Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC)
. While DPoP operates at the application layer to secure API tokens for public and confidential clients, DBSC operates at the browser and network layer to cryptographically bind browser session cookies to the device's hardware (such as TPM). Together, DPoP and DBSC form a comprehensive defense-in-depth strategy against credential theft across both API and web-based user sessions.
Multi-Agent Delegation & Model Context Protocol (MCP)
As autonomous AI agents and
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
architectures emerge, securing tool-use tokens becomes critical. While DPoP is highly resilient in single-hop client-to-server connections, multi-agent workflows (where Agent A delegates a task to Agent B, which calls Resource C) introduce delegation challenges.
In a multi-agent chain, Agent B cannot sign a DPoP proof on behalf of Agent A without access to Agent A's private key—and sharing private keys violates the core security principles of DPoP. Because Google's core consumer OAuth endpoint (oauth2.googleapis.com) does not support
OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693)
, developers building multi-agent or federated cloud workloads should consider
Google Cloud Secure Token Service (STS)
. By routing delegation through STS, the intermediate agent can exchange the upstream token for a new, short-lived federated token cryptographically bound to its own local key pair, preserving the sender-constrained security model across the entire agent chain without key exposure.
See our
DPoP Adoption Guide
, our DPoP adoption

, and improve your platform security today.

Evaluating AI agents: moving past the vibe check
- Google Developers Blog
Evaluating AI agents: moving past the vibe check
OCT. 15, 2026
Hugo Selbie
Customer & Partner Solutions Engineer
Dani Zamora
Solutions Engineer
Jesse Carah
Incubation Lead
John DeMartino
Staff Customer & Partner Solutions Engineer
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
TL;DR
Your agent can loop, burn tokens, or give a completely hallucinated answer and still look fine. A vibe check won't catch that. This post is the playbook behind our AI Agent Clinic episode
How to Actually Evaluate (Any) AI Agent: Beyond the Vibe Check
, where we build an eval pipeline for a LangGraph agent in 60 minutes. Here's what's inside:
Evaluating AI agents: moving past the vibe check
When teams start building an AI agent, testing usually looks the same. You wire up a model, hand it a few tools, run three or four prompts in a terminal, and eyeball the output. If the answer looks reasonable, you ship it.
In practice, this breaks down fast. You tweak a system prompt to fix an edge case in one workflow, and suddenly the agent stops calling a required tool in another.
Worse, agents fail differently than standard software. An agent can get stuck in a retry loop, fire off multiple tool calls, yet still return a polite, plausible-sounding final answer.
In production, that hidden failure is costly:
It quietly spikes your cloud bill and token usage.
It exhausts downstream API rate limits and quotas.
It leaves users staring at a loading spinner.
It can trigger duplicate side effects in external systems, all while looking "fine" on the surface.
It erodes user trust, and first impressions are hard to win back.
Integrating a reliable evaluation suite into your development lifecycle can seem like extra overhead during initial prototyping, right up until modifying your system prompt causes unexpected breaking changes. The key is recognizing that evaluation is a progressive journey: any repeatable evaluation system (no matter how simple) is better than relying on ad-hoc spot checks or no system at all. You don't need an elaborate automated grading architecture on Day 0. Instead, start with simple, repeatable checks and evolve your evaluation into a more complex, automated framework as your agent's capabilities and production demands grow.
Establishing a repeatable evaluation system is made substantially easier by integrating these decisions into an evaluation framework. Transitioning beyond simple subjective checks relies on two core pillars: human oversight and targeted tools. In this article, we explore how to set up an evaluation framework using the open-source
agent-eval
toolkit. We'll demonstrate how combining manually reviewed traces with automated verification helps detect silent regressions early in development and scales seamlessly as your agent transitions to production.
Getting started: the high-level building blocks
1. Define success with critical user journeys
Before writing test code, you need a shared vision of what a good outcome actually looks like. Anchor your tests in
critical user journeys (CUJs)
rather than abstract benchmarks.
A CUJ defines what a user expects the system to achieve, structured around their persona, goals, constraints, and verification conditions:
"As an operations analyst, I expect the agent to ingest a counterparty trade discrepancy email, identify the disputed transaction, verify the trade economics against our internal ledger within 30 seconds, and draft a response reverse-translating our internal trade IDs back into the broker's nomenclature without human intervention."
Every clause in that statement becomes an evaluation point: Did the agent resolve the correct transaction ID? Did it check the ledger before drafting? Did it map internal IDs back to the external nomenclature?
Every clause of a CUJ becomes an evaluation point.
Defining these expectations upfront forces product stakeholders, downstream users, and engineers to agree on defining how “success” is measured.
2. Start with simulated users, graduate to real traffic
You do not need six months of production logs to build your initial golden dataset. Instead, break each CUJ down into concrete
scenarios
(both happy paths and edge cases) and feed them into a
user simulator LLM
(we like
ADK user simulations
). Primed with a persona and behavioral constraints (for example, an impatient analyst giving incomplete ticket numbers, or a developer asking a multi-part debugging question), the simulator mirrors the messy phrasing, typos, and multi-turn complexity of real users.
Example scenarios for ADK user simulations.
By testing your agent against a synthetic user and realistic scenarios, you can record comprehensive execution traces (including tool logs) prior to user interaction. This enables you to pinpoint and resolve any performance gaps against your release standards. As live traffic begins to flow, you can progressively replace these synthetic setups with real production traces.
3. Measure across the full stack
A single top-line score will never tell you
why
an agent failed. To isolate root causes, layer four types of checks: unit tests, deterministic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge rubrics, and integration tests.
Four layers of checks, from unit tests to integration tests.
Four common traps to avoid
Trap 1: Throwing tests out and breaking your baseline
Setting up evaluation metrics involves trial and error, and it is tempting to delete a noisy test or swap out sample queries between runs. Every time you add or remove a test, though, you invalidate your baseline: you cannot tell if a score changed because the agent got better or because the test suite moved. Keep your golden dataset frozen while you tune a feature, change one variable at a time, and only retire a test when you are certain the underlying requirement has changed.
Deleting tests moves the baseline, not the agent.
Trap 2: Relying on fuzzy 1-to-5 judge scores instead of boolean checks
LLMs are notoriously inconsistent at grading qualitative 1-to-5 scales; the boundary between a "3" and a "4" is fuzzy and often shifts from run to run.
Whenever possible, turn your judge rubrics into
boolean (pass/fail) questions
rather than open-ended rating scales. Rather than asking
"How helpful was this answer from 1 to 5?"
, ask
"Did the agent verify the account ID before calling the refund tool? (Yes/No)"
. (We like
Adaptive Rubrics
)
Trap 3: Evaluating the prose while ignoring the operational bill
A response that passes every quality check is still a production failure if it took 40 seconds, made twelve redundant tool calls, and cost sixty cents per query.
Always evaluate the whole system rather than just the final text. Track
latency, token consumption (prompt, reasoning, and completion tokens), API cost, and tool-call counts
right alongside answer quality.
Trap 4: Building a different eval pipeline for a different agentic framework
Switching orchestration frameworks often forces teams to scrap and rewrite their entire testing suite. While most frameworks emit OpenTelemetry traces, they don’t use the same semantic conventions for tool calls, steps, and tokens. Standardizing your traces around open specifications like
OpenInference
solves this by decoupling evaluation from your orchestration framework. Tools like the
agent-eval toolkit
support this natively, with minimal setup.
A practical Day 0 to Day 2 rollout
You do not need to build an observability platform from scratch. You can stand up the evaluation pipeline in a couple of hours using open-source utilities like the
agent-eval toolkit
which pairs OpenTelemetry trace capture with the Agent Evaluation service on the Gemini platform (formerly Vertex AI Evaluation). But building your actual evaluation strategy requires more thought.
Day 0: Scenarios, simulations, and the "red pen"
Start small and stay close to the raw data:
Draft scenarios covering your main CUJs and run simulations through your agent.
Ignore aggregate scores and read the actual execution traces from top to bottom: the prompts, intermediate reasoning steps, tool arguments, and final outputs.
Grade the traces with a
red pen
, marking every spot where the agent hesitated, hallucinated a parameter, picked the wrong tool, or rambled.
One agent trace, graded with a red pen.
Why the red pen matters:
Manually reading twenty traces feels slow compared to auto-generating a chart, but it saves days of wasted effort. Instead of guessing at hypothetical failure modes and writing generic rubrics that miss the mark, an hour with a red pen shows you how your system actually breaks in reality. Aggregating those notes gives you a high-signal list of the exact deterministic assertions and boolean judge checks you need to build next.
Day 1: Cadence, signal, and the testing framework
Once you have that initial list of checks, tools like
agent-eval toolkit
takes over the heavy lifting and standardizes execution. Helping you with things like:
Scaffolding and execution:
Scaffold your golden dataset and execute multi-turn scenarios against your agent over HTTP (--
base-url
) or offline.
Framework-agnostic trace ingestion:
Get structured OpenTelemetry traces with OpenInference conventions, whether you build with Google ADK, LangGraph, or a custom runtime.
Agent Evaluation integration:
Routes those traces into the Agent Evaluation service on Gemini platform to run your deterministic checks and boolean judge rubrics without bespoke API code.
Establish a regular cadence of runs with your eval pipeline:
Run on every change:
Whenever you adjust a prompt, swap a model, or edit a tool docstring, execute the exact same test battery and compare the delta against your baseline.
Metrics over time in the agent-eval HTML report.
Validate the judge against your traces:
Never trust a new LLM-as-a-judge metric blindly. Compare the automated scores against the traces you graded by hand on Day 0. If the judge gives a passing score to a trace you marked up with red ink, tighten the grading prompt until the automated signal matches your engineering judgment.
The tuning loop: 50 to 60 iterations of turning knobs, not rewrites
Once your Day 1 framework is active, optimization becomes a disciplined, mechanical loop:
One turn of the tuning loop on a sample agent.
In a real deployment, reaching production quality often takes 50 to 60 small iterations. You are not rewriting the entire system prompt every morning; you are gradually turning individual knobs. One tweak clarifies a tool parameter description. The next adds a negative constraint. The next adjusts the JSON output schema.
For instance, upon completion of each evaluation run, the
agent-eval
framework constructs an
interactive, all-in-one HTML report
. This report aligns pass/fail boolean metrics alongside key operational metrics, including latency, token usage, API expenditure, cache utilization, and detailed tool-call execution paths. Additionally, it incorporates automated Gemini root-cause analyses for failed conversational turns, pinpointing the exact prompt directive or parameter setting that triggered the failure to guide your next adjustment.
That data replaces hunches. A prompt change might feel much smarter in manual spot-checking, only for the test battery to reveal that latency doubled and tool-call hallucinations ticked up by 15%.
The lesson for teams building agents:
small, measured changes beat big rewrites every time.
Day 2: Merge gates and shared dashboards
Once you trust the signal coming out of your eval pipeline, turn it into a permanent regression safety net:
CI/CD pull request gates with headless CLI:
Execute tools like agent-eval headlessly in your build pipeline (such as Cloud Build or GitHub Actions). On every pull request, it runs your golden dataset and enforces two merge rules:
A global pass threshold:
The suite must meet a minimum pass bar (for example, 95% boolean success).
Zero regressions on core evaluation metrics:
Even if the overall score holds steady, the build fails if any previously passing metric regresses. This prevents developers from accidentally trading a critical capability for a minor edge-case improvement.
Shared dashboards and centralized storage:
Configure your eval processes to export run artifacts—including raw trace JSONL, prompt hashes, model versions, latency profiles, and scorecard summaries—into a central data warehouse like BigQuery or Cloud Storage. Publishing these metrics to a shared team dashboard gives everyone visibility into accuracy, latency percentiles, and token budgets across releases.
After launch, real production traces flow back into the golden dataset.
See it in action
Link to Youtube Video
(visible only when JS is disabled)
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wPdoZRbvaF4
Watch the walkthrough:
Check out our companion video,
How to Actually Evaluate (Any) AI Agent: Beyond the Vibe Check
, where we build this whole pipeline live on a real LangGraph agent, in 60 minutes.
Grab the code:
Clone the open-source
agent-eval toolkit on GitHub
to scaffold datasets, collect traces, and generate diagnostic HTML reports out of the box.
The Outer Loop, Insights First: An Ambient Quality Agent That Diagnoses Your Production Agent.
Frequently asked questions
What are the issues with manual "vibe checks" for AI agents?
Running three or four prompts in a terminal only shows you the final text response. An agent can loop on retries, hallucinate tool parameters, burn token budgets, or trigger duplicate side effects while still returning a polite answer. Automated trace evaluation checks intermediate tool calls, state transitions, latency percentiles, and API cost alongside answer quality so silent regressions don't ship.
How do I evaluate an AI agent from scratch?
Treat evaluation as a progressive rollout from Day 0 to Day 2 rather than an all-or-nothing jump. On
Day 0
, break your critical user journeys (CUJs) into a handful of test scenarios and run them through
ADK user simulations
. Read those first 5 to 20 execution traces with a "red pen" to see where the agent hesitates, picks the wrong tool, or rambles.
On
Day 1
, turn those red-pen notes into automated checks so you can tune one variable at a time. Once your pass rates stabilize, lock those checks into
Day 2
CI/CD pull request gates.
Why use boolean (pass/fail) checks instead of 1-to-5 rating scales for LLM-as-a-judge?
LLM judges don't grade 1-to-5 scales consistently because the boundary between a "3" and a "4" shifts from run to run. With
Adaptive Rubrics
, you split broad quality goals into strict Yes/No questions like
"Did the agent verify the account ID before refunding?"
Pair those boolean rubrics with deterministic
computation metrics
for tool parameters and reference checks, plus trace assertions for latency and token budgets.
Can I use the same evaluation pipeline across LangGraph, Google ADK, and custom agent frameworks?
Yes, if you decouple your evaluation pipeline from your agent framework by standardizing OpenTelemetry traces on
OpenInference
semantic conventions. The open-source
agent-eval toolkit
routes those traces straight to the Agent Evaluation service on the Gemini platform (formerly Vertex AI Evaluation). You don't have to rewrite grading code when switching orchestration frameworks.
What happens after my agent is deployed to production?
Once your Day 2 pipeline exports traces and scorecards to BigQuery or Cloud Storage, you can compare live traffic against your pre-production baseline. When users hit edge cases your initial scenarios missed,
ambient quality agents like The Outer Loop
help you diagnose those failing production traces. You can then promote those real traces straight into your Day 0 golden dataset so your test suite evolves with live usage.

By Mistral

Thinking
Summary
Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.
Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.
Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.
Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM)
Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.
Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.
Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.
Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.
Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.
Benchmark Results
We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.
GIFT-Eval - GMean MASE
GIFT-Eval - GMean WQL
GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.
TIME - GMean MASE
TIME - GMean CRPS
TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.
fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.
Family of models optimised for every specification
Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.
Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.
Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.
An industrial example
Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.
Multivariate forecasting.
A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.
Probabilistic forecasting.
A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.
Categorical covariates.
Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.
Known-future covariates.
Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.
From Model to System
Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.
In the plant, that could look like this:
Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.
When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.
The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.
The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.
The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.
Key technical contributions
Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.
Decoupled Horizon Forecasting.
Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.
Covariate-aware attention.
Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.
Synthetic-first data.
The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.
Two-stage training.
Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.
A model that can be adapted
Public benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.
For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through
Mistral Forge
, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:
Zero-shot inference
out of the box.
Architectural extensions
, such as domain-specific covariates.
Fine-tuning on proprietary data
, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.
Control over the training data
, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.
The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.
What’s next
We have published a
GitHub repository
so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.

Open-sourcing SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer
See a demo
Try Perplexity
Open-sourcing SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer
Perplexity open-sources SPACE, the sandbox platform behind Computer, to help developers build safer autonomous AI agents
Oct 15, 2026
Since launching
Computer
in February, Perplexity has been an early pioneer in personal agents. Weâre committed to the hard problems of agent governance, detecting unsafe behaviors and preventing rogue agent activity. In July, we replaced our commercially available sandbox provider with a more robust and resilient in-house solution we named
SPACE
.
SPACE provides high security for advanced agentic systems. In fact, a recent
barrage of security testing
proved SPACE resilient against network-bypass techniques like those used in the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident.
Today, we're open-sourcing SPACE to give developers a foundation for building safer agent systems and contributing to stronger protections across the industry. Developers can access the
repository here
.
Agent governance is an engineering problem
, and open source is essential to solving it. When developers have systems they can inspect, adapt, and build on, they find more weaknesses and develop better tools. Open-sourcing SPACE gives developers a production-tested foundation for agent runtimes, with isolation, state recovery, and credential and network controls built in.
Creating a foundation for other builders
Sandboxes keep agents secure, letting them access the tools and files they need to complete these tasks, while keeping sensitive information protected.
Open-sourcing SPACE gives developers a starting point for the environments where their agents run code and work with files. Teams can see how the SPACE sandbox platform works and build on its implementation. They can also adapt it to their needs rather than recreating the underlying infrastructure.
In Computer, SPACE supports isolated code execution, pause and resume, recovery, and session branching. Those capabilities provide the foundation for assistants that could:
Analyze data:
Clean a spreadsheet, run calculations, and create charts in a separate workspace.
Resume work:
Pause for someone to review a draft or supply missing information, then resume with their files and running state preserved.
Explore alternatives:
Test two ways to clean a dataset in separate copies of their workspace, or restore an earlier file after a mistake.
These examples illustrate how developers could use SPACE's documented isolation and session controls. Platform and security engineers can also review the isolation model and security examples before integrating SPACE into their own systems.
Increasing security for autonomous work
When we give agents more room to solve problems, we need
clear limits
on how they do it. We know that agents pursuing legitimate tasks can still cross security boundaries when they attempt to work around missing files, failed requests, or permission denials.
We can put model safeguards into place to reduce the likelihood of unsafe behavior. Adding independent controls in the surrounding system helps contain the damage if those safeguards fail. They limit what an agent can access regardless of what it decides to do.
SPACE puts those controls around a separate workspace for agent-generated code and files. We designed it to combine isolation, recovery, and efficient execution. This lets agents perform useful work over long sessions without relying on the model alone to respect security boundaries.
Running inside its own operating system
Each SPACE sandbox runs inside a small virtual machine with its own operating system, creating an isolation boundary between the agentâs work and the host system. A central control plane coordinates when these workspaces are created, paused, resumed, or removed.
SPACE treats the sandbox as untrusted and manages network access and platform-held credentials outside the sandbox. Agents can connect to authorized services without those credentials being stored in their working environment.
Frequent file snapshots
and checkpoints of the full running environment preserve progress across interruptions. To keep these operations efficient, SPACE stores changes rather than repeatedly copying entire environments. This reduces the work needed to create, restore, or branch a sandbox.
Improving production performance
Since July, SPACE has powered all Computer sessions and has handled millions of sandbox creations per day.
In a comparison
on the same production traffic, sandbox creation was three to five times faster than with our previous provider.
We also
tested SPACE
against agents deliberately trying to breach its boundaries. Our published security evaluation found no escape from the virtual machine to the host in 108 attempts, but some found ways around network restrictions. We fixed those weaknesses, and neither identified attack method succeeded in follow-up testing.
We also disclosed related weaknesses we found in other sandbox platforms to their vendors, extending that work beyond our own infrastructure.
Contributing to safer agentic AI
SPACE is part of a broader effort to strengthen the systems people rely on as AI takes on more work. Through the
Secure Intelligence Institute
, we conduct security research and collaborate with the wider community, translating findings into practical defenses.
We believe open-sourcing security tools gives developers more ways to test defenses, find weaknesses, and build safer AI systems. We've shared tools that address different parts of that work:
BrowseSafe
, a model and benchmark for detecting malicious instructions hidden in web pages.
Numbat
, a security toolkit, open-sourced in July, that helps detect, investigate, and prevent dangerous agent behavior on computers
Bumblebee
, a scanner open-sourced in May, that checks developer machines for risky software packages, extensions, and AI tool configurations
Making these tools available lets other teams inspect our work, adapt it to their needs, and contribute improvements. With SPACE, we're extending that approach to the environments where agents execute code and work with files.
Deploying for agent systems
Akamai
has tested and launched SPACE on its cloud platform and is working with Perplexity to bring it to its customers.
Crusoe
is also partnering with Perplexity to add SPACE to its Managed AI Services portfolio.
CoreWeave
has published setup guidance for developers who want to deploy SPACE for evaluation on
CKS
.
Developers can start with the SPACEâs setup instructions and security guidance to deploy it for their own agent systems. The
repository
and
documentation
define the supported configurations and included components.

Rollouts and Security Review
Today we're launching two Cursor bots for the last mile of shipping code. Rollouts watches every change as it deploys and reports its health per environment. Security Review reports exploitable bugs on every pull request.
Both are available today on Teams and Enterprise plans.
#
Rollouts
Rollouts attaches a monitor to every pull request and watches the change as it deploys, reporting change health per environment: verified healthy, regression detected, or inconclusive. It's the Cursor version of
Firetiger
Change Monitors, rebuilt with the Bot Development Kit.
Enable it from the dashboard and connect source control, your deploy system, and your telemetry provider. Rollouts starts watching on the next pull request.
#
Monitoring plans
When a pull request opens, Rollouts reads the diff and the systems it touches, then writes a monitoring plan as a PR comment. The plan lists the risks it identified, the effect the change is meant to have, the signals it will check, and any gaps in instrumentation that would make the change hard to verify. Edit the plan in the PR and Rollouts uses your version.
#
Deploy tracking
Rollouts wakes on deploy events for the change's commit and runs the plan against your logs, metrics, and traces. It tracks each environment separately, so a change can be verified in staging and still flagged in production. Rollouts checks the change's intended effect alongside error and latency signals, and reports back on the PR when it reaches a verdict.
#
Regressions
When Rollouts detects a regression, it names the change it suspects and notifies the author. Depending on configuration, it can also open a revert PR for review or hand the finding to a cloud agent for a fix. Rollouts does not merge or roll back on its own today.
#
Integrations
Rollouts connects to Origin or GitHub for source control, to your continuous delivery system for deploy events, and to Datadog and other telemetry providers for signals. Feature flag integration is coming soon.
#
Security Review
Security Review is available today. It reads every pull request in the context of the codebase and posts one review comment reporting exploitable bugs. Style and quality stay with Bugbot.
Enable it from the dashboard for the repositories you want reviewed. Draft PRs are skipped.
#
What it reports
Security Review looks for injection across SQL, command, and template surfaces, along with authentication and authorization bypasses, including checks that a refactor stopped running. It also flags secrets and credentials committed to source, SSRF and unvalidated redirects, unsafe deserialization, and dependency changes that introduce known vulnerabilities. It traces where user input enters and what it passes through.
#
Findings
Each finding carries a severity, the attack path, and a proposed fix. Dismiss one with a reason and Security Review won't raise it again on that PR.
#
Team rules
Add rules for your codebase, such as which client external calls must go through or which tables are never queried from a request handler, and Security Review enforces them on every PR.
#
Get started

automations
tab.

Today, we're releasing North Small Translate, a mixture-of-experts machine translation model with strong performance across 50+ languages. Across WMT26 benchmarks,¹ North Small Translate achieves an 83.6 score across all languages, outperforming proprietary models like DeepL and Google Translate, as well as open-weight alternatives such as Gemma 4 31B (off), GLM 5.2, and Mistral Large 3.
North Small Translate marks a significant milestone as Cohere's first translation model in the North model family. It builds on our multilingual and translation lineage — from the
Tiny Aya model family
to
Command A Translate
— and represents a clear next step in Cohere’s commitment to offering high-quality machine translation wherever it is needed.

North Small Translate outperforms similarly sized open-weight models under 1T parameters and API-based translation models in various dimensions of machine translation on average. In WMT model evaluations, North Small Translate leads with an WMT26 All Languages benchmark score of 83.60, compared with 81.56 for Qwen 3.5 397B A17B, 76.50 for GLM 5.2 FP8, 81.37 for DeepL NextGen, 79.46 for Gemma 4 31B (on), and 68.20 for Google Translate. North Small Translate performs strongly across 32 high-resource languages and 18 additional languages. North Small Translate is the most consistent performer across the full spread of regions, without the sharp regional drop-offs seen in other models of its size. On average across all languages, it is the best-performing dedicated machine translation model in this evaluation — open or closed.
Image 2: Overall WMT scores by regional average across DeepL, Google Translate, and Gemma 31B (on), and North Small Translate using GPT-5.6-Sol as a judge.
At the regional level, North Small Translate punches above its weight, beating Gemma 4 31B (on) outright in Europe (82.2 vs. 73.9) while running essentially even with it in South Asia (86.2 vs. 86.7).
At the regional level, both North Small Translate and its Agentic counterpart beat Gemma 4 31B (on) outright across Europe — EU languages (82.74 Agentic / 82.17 standard vs. 72.73) and non-EU European languages (81.52 / 81.24 vs. 75.90) — while running essentially even with it in South Asia (87.13 / 86.16 vs. 88.04).
Both versions also outperform DeepL NextGen across every non-European region tested — MENA, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and East Asia — with the largest advantage in South Asia and MENA (roughly 8–10 points ahead of DeepL), a moderate edge in Southeast Asia (about 4–5 points), and the narrowest edge in East Asia (about 1-3 points, with the standard model closing in on DeepL's 85.41 score).
Increased throughput for faster workflows
North Small Translate is built for high-throughput generation, prioritizing raw output speed even as concurrency scales.
In our testing, North Small Translate achieved up to 1.4x higher output throughput than Gemma 4 31B TP1 (1 x GPU) under identical concurrency levels and hardware configurations — 112 vs. 81 Output Tokens per Second (TOPS) at low concurrency and 39 vs. 30 TOPS at high concurrency. In practical terms, that's 30-38% more tokens generated per second, translating to meaningfully faster completion times on longer outputs.
Image 3: North Small Translate’s output speed compared to Gemma 4 31B (off), across high and low concurrencies, in internal tests on identical hardware.
Long documents are where many translation models fall apart, and North Small Translate isn't one of them. It scores 48.9 on our long-context evaluation, more than double Google Translate (21.3) and Gemma 4 31B (19.4), and ahead of every general-purpose LLM we tested.³
Paired with its throughput advantage, that means fast, reliable translation at length, without the quality collapse seen in most non-specialized alternatives.
Efficient cost of translation, at scale
Efficiency is a core constraint in enterprise translation deployment, and we engineered North Small Translate to be extremely cost-efficient, without sacrificing performance.
Image 4: Overall WMT score and cost per task breakdown across machine translation models, using pricing per token or character from model providers' websites.
For enterprises evaluating commercial licenses of North Small Translate, benefit from a strong 80.1 score at just $0.000676 per task, using only 661 tokens on average. Compared to Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (high) — which costs $0.038928 per task (5,762% more than North Small Translate).
Similarly sized models like Qwen 3.5 397B A17B and Cohere’s own Command A+ have decent performance at $0.004525 and $0.005158 per task, respectively.
Best in translation, in partnership with RWS
North Small Translate was developed in partnership with
RWS
, an AI solutions company pioneering in language technology and services. Close collaboration with RWS, specifically Language Weaver’s research and science teams along with its language experts, helped shape the model's real-world translation performance throughout development. RWS works with more than 80% of the world’s top 100 brands, empowering the world's most ambitious brands to communicate seamlessly across borders and cultures.
For enterprises that need more than open-weight research access, security, scalability, and a dedicated translation and localization platform, North Small Translate, is available through RWS’s
Language Weaver
product.
Getting Started
North Small Translate is available today on
Hugging Face
for non-commercial and research use. Visit our
documentation
for detailed model specs, deployment guides, and implementation examples to get started. For information about how the model was developed, read our
technical report
.
Footnotes
¹
WMT Benchmarks
focus on evaluation of general capabilities of machine translation (MT) systems. Its primary goal is to test performance across a wide range of languages, domains, genres, and modalities.
² To understand WMT Benchmark scores, the scoring methodology defines performance ranges as follows: 0-20 (not acceptable), 20-40 (borderline), 40-60 (acceptable), 60-80 (good with major errors), and 80-100 (perfect or with minor errors).
³ Long context evaluation measures how well a model can translate two chapters of a book on a single call. The quality is measured for each paragraph in isolation via xComet-XL metrics.
